summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct through its own courts. The High Court struck down the colonial-era "carnal knowledge" offence on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021, writing that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The repealed sections were formally struck from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026, deleting paragraphs (a) and (c) of Section 164.

Penal Code Section 167, which addresses same-sex conduct between women, was not removed by that litigation. In the Universal Periodic Review of May 2023 (43rd session), Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to repeal Section 167 and also declined a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition; the outcome records that "a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced."

Legal gender recognition has been won case by case rather than granted by statute. In September 2017 the High Court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment (ND v Attorney General). In December 2017 the High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time: Tshepo Ricki Kgositau obtained a female identity card after a four-year legal battle, having undergone gender confirmation surgery in December 2016, and dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." The trans legal-gender right was confirmed across 2017 to 2022.

In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation, which legal commentator Carmel Rickard said gives LGBTQ Batswana "an even stronger, constitutionally-based argument" against discrimination.

A draft constitutional amendment under consideration in June 2024 would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct, and civic groups criticised the wider review process.

Implementation of Botswana's precedent wins has not been satisfactory, according to the Southern Africa Litigation Centre writing in May 2024, which cited the 2016 Court of Appeal order registering LEGABIBO, the 2017 identity-document ruling and the 2021 decriminalisation judgment together.

Official hostility has been recorded alongside official protection. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. President Ian Khama deported American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi acknowledged that people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his 10 years in office while declining to change the law he said would lose him an election.

Enforcement history is thin. Same-sex acts remained illegal until June 2019 but prosecution was rare, and the U.S. State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found police "did not target same-sex activity" and recorded no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year, while documenting societal discrimination against LGBT people. LEGABIBO and activists called the Government's 2019 appeal an "affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia." Afrobarometer tolerance rose from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021 among respondents welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour.
tangentialFactors:
Botswana's constitutional framework is doing work that statute has not: the June 2019 reading of "sex" in Section 3 to cover sexual orientation gives litigants a constitutional route against discrimination even where the Penal Code still contains Section 167.

The draft constitutional amendment of 2024 covers intersex persons and people with disabilities but its sponsors have kept intersex and same-sex provisions separate, and civic groups have criticised the wider review process, so the amendment's trajectory is unresolved.

Public tolerance as measured by Afrobarometer moved from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021 welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour, a majority still not reached.

Regional comparison: the Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed implementation of precedent wins across Botswana and Namibia together as "not been satisfactory so far" as of May 2024.
localsOnly:
LEGABIBO is Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation, legally registered following the 2016 Court of Appeal order, and runs advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work including World AIDS Day commemorations, with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources on its site.

Residents have a functioning community infrastructure to approach for support, alongside the case-by-case gender-recognition route through the High Court.

Former President Festus Mogae's instruction to police not to arrest or harass gay people during his decade in office, and President Mokgweetsi Masisi's November 2018 statement acknowledging violations suffered by people in same-sex relationships, are statements of executive posture rather than statutory protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the March 2026 Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order has been challenged or is subject to any pending litigation is not sourced here.

Whether Section 167 has been the basis of any actual prosecution, and at what point, is unresolved in this inventory; the sources establish only that it was not repealed and that Botswana declined to repeal it at the 2023 UPR.

The current status of the 2024 draft constitutional amendment, including whether the intersex provision has been enacted, is unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses airport or border screening, document inspection at entry, or access to gender-affirming healthcare for visitors; those remain not sourced.

The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's assessment that implementation "has not been satisfactory" does not specify which of the three cited judgments went unimplemented, and that detail is unresolved here.
